questiontext.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes a storage device and a filesystem?

answer.text: A device holds data; a filesystem organizes files, directories, and metadata in a storage area
A filesystem is a physical drive and a device is a directory path
They are two names for a mount point
A storage device is always a partition table

questiontext.text: What is a partition?

answer.text: A logical region of a storage device
A directory where a filesystem is attached
A compressed archive of home files
A unique name assigned to a regular user

questiontext.text: What is a mount point?

answer.text: A directory where a filesystem is attached to the Linux directory tree
A block of free space at the end of a disk
The UUID of a user account
A location reserved only for archives

questiontext.text: When a filesystem is mounted over a directory, any files previously visible underneath that mount point are hidden until it is unmounted.

answer.text: true
false

questiontext.text: What is lsblk -f primarily used to inspect in this lesson?

answer.text: Block-device relationships and filesystem details such as type, label, UUID, and mount point
Directory permissions throughout the home folder
The contents of a compressed tar archive
How many words are in every mounted filesystem

questiontext.text: What kind of information can blkid report?

answer.text: Filesystem type and metadata tokens such as labels or UUIDs
The contents of each file on a partition
The number of running processes using a disk
Whether a directory contains hidden files

questiontext.text: An unprivileged user may see only cached, unverified information from blkid.

answer.text: true
false

questiontext.text: What is a filesystem UUID?

answer.text: An identifier associated with a filesystem
A mount command that formats a partition
The amount of space used by a directory
The name of the root user's home directory

questiontext.text: What does mount with no arguments display?

answer.text: Currently mounted filesystems and their mount points
All unformatted devices that could be mounted
Only the available space in the user's home directory
A list of partitions sorted by size

questiontext.text: Why should students not run mount DEVICE DIRECTORY in this lab?

answer.text: It attempts to attach a filesystem and changes system state
It lists files without changing anything
It creates a compressed backup automatically
It only prints the device UUID

questiontext.text: What does df -h "$HOME" report?

answer.text: Used and available space on the filesystem containing the home path, in human-readable units
Only the total size of files directly in the home directory
The filesystem type and UUID of every partition
The contents of all archive files under home

questiontext.text: What does du -sh directory summarize?

answer.text: Estimated space attributed to files under the directory, summarized in human-readable form
Available capacity of the entire physical device only
Filesystem labels and UUIDs below the directory
The number of mounted filesystems

questiontext.text: Why might df and du report different amounts?

answer.text: They measure different things, and metadata, reserved space, snapshots, links, sparse files, or compression can affect totals
df counts words while du counts users
They always inspect different physical devices
du reports only free space on a mounted filesystem

questiontext.text: In the lesson's tar options, what does -c request?

answer.text: Create an archive
Compare filesystem capacity
Change the mount point
Count files below a directory

questiontext.text: What does tar -tzf archive.tar.gz do?

answer.text: Lists the gzip-compressed tar archive contents without extracting them
Creates a new filesystem on a partition
Deletes the archive after listing it
Restores files into the root directory

questiontext.text: What does tar -xzf archive.tar.gz -C restore-test do?

answer.text: Extracts the gzip-compressed archive after changing to restore-test
Creates an archive from restore-test
Lists all mounted filesystems below restore-test
Moves restore-test to a new partition

questiontext.text: In the examples, what does the -f option specify for tar?

answer.text: The archive filename
The filesystem type
The number of source files
The output's human-readable units

questiontext.text: What does the -z option request in these tar examples?

answer.text: Use gzip compression or decompression
Sort archive paths alphabetically
Use a UUID as the output filename
Overwrite every mounted filesystem

questiontext.text: What does -C restore-test do in the extraction example?

answer.text: Changes to restore-test before extracting the archive
Creates the restore-test directory automatically in every case
Compresses the archive using a different algorithm
Checks the filesystem capacity of restore-test

questiontext.text: Extracting a practice archive into a new, empty directory helps avoid overwriting unrelated files.

answer.text: true
false

questiontext.text: Why should a student test-extract an archive after listing its contents?

answer.text: A restore test checks that files can be extracted and inspected, not only that entry names are listed
Listing an archive changes the source files
Extraction is required to calculate the filesystem UUID
A listing always removes incomplete archive entries

questiontext.text: Why is an archive stored on the same device as its source not an independent backup?

answer.text: The same device failure, theft, malware, or mistake could affect both copies
An archive can never be restored from a local disk
Tar archives must be stored only in /boot
The source directory becomes a mount point

questiontext.text: Which statement best distinguishes an archive from a backup?

answer.text: An archive bundles selected files; a backup is a separate recoverable copy intended to support restoration
Every archive is automatically a protected off-site backup
A backup is a mount command that attaches a partition
They are identical terms for filesystem labels

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes formatting and mounting?

answer.text: Formatting creates a filesystem and can overwrite data; mounting makes an existing filesystem accessible at a path
Formatting lists current mounts; mounting estimates directory size
They are both read-only inspection commands
Mounting always creates a backup of the device

questiontext.text: Why might the mount listing contain entries such as /proc or /sys?

answer.text: Virtual filesystems can provide kernel, process, or device information without representing a physical disk
Every mount point corresponds to a removable USB drive
They are directories created by the tar command
They are all partitions that have not been formatted

questiontext.text: Which activity fits the safety scope of this lesson?

answer.text: Inspect current device and mount information, then archive files created in the lab directory
Format the first device shown by lsblk
Run dd to overwrite a block device with zeros
Mount an unknown partition over /home

questiontext.text: Which statement about filesystems is accurate?

answer.text: Different systems and devices may use different filesystem types for compatibility, reliability, or feature needs
Every Linux filesystem uses one universal format
A partition and a filesystem always mean the same thing
Filesystem type can only be identified from a filename extension

questiontext.text: Which action strengthens a backup plan?

answer.text: Store a protected copy separately from the source and periodically test restoring it
Keep the only archive beside the original and never inspect it
Assume a successful creation command proves every file can be restored
Save sensitive data in a public location without access controls

questiontext.text: The forms of lsblk -f, df -h, du -sh, and mount with no arguments used in this lesson are for inspection and do not partition or format storage.

answer.text: true
false

questiontext.text: Why does the lab restrict du to a small practice directory?

answer.text: Scanning a large tree can take time and may cross into data outside the exercise scope
du formats every directory it scans
du can only read files under /home
A small path causes it to return a filesystem UUID

questiontext.text: A filesystem UUID can identify a filesystem independently of a device's temporary name.

answer.text: true
false

questiontext.text: A system has a root filesystem mounted at / and a separate filesystem mounted at /home. Which statement is correct?

answer.text: Both filesystems appear within one directory tree at their respective mount points
The filesystem at /home replaces the root filesystem permanently
The /home filesystem cannot contain directories
Each filesystem must have a separate shell
